rows.stem: The magnitude of the electric field due to a point charge object at a distance of 4.0 m is 9 N/C. From the same charged object the electric field of magnitude, \(16\,\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\) will be at a distance of
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "1. ( c ) 3 m", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The field of a point charge falls off as the inverse square of the distance, \(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}\), so for the same charge \(E_1 r_1^{2} = E_2 r_2^{2}\).

\(9 \times (4.0)^{2} = 16 \times r^{2}\), so \(r^{2} = \dfrac{144}{16} = 9\) and \(r = 3\) m.

That is the keyed option, 3 m.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem: A point P lies at a distance \(x\) from the mid point of an electric dipole on its axis. The electric potential at point P is proportional to
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "2. ( a ) \(1/x^{2}\)", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

For a short dipole of moment \(p\), the potential at a point on the axis a distance \(x\) from the centre is \(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{x^{2}}\).

The quickest way to see the power is to add the two point-charge potentials directly. With charges \(+q\) and \(-q\) separated by \(2a\), the axial potential is \(V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-a} - \dfrac{1}{x+a}\right) = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2a}{x^{2}-a^{2}}\), which for \(x \gg a\) becomes \(\dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^{2}}\).

So the potential is proportional to \(1/x^{2}\), the keyed option. Note that the dipole FIELD on the axis goes as \(1/x^{3}\); it is the potential that goes as \(1/x^{2}\), which is what this question is testing.

rows.stem: A current of 0.8 A flows in a conductor of 40 \(\Omega\) for 1 minute. The heat produced in the conductor will be
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "3. ( b ) 1536 J", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Joule heating in a resistor is \(H = I^{2}Rt\). Here \(I = 0.8\) A, \(R = 40\,\Omega\) and \(t = 1\) minute \(= 60\) s, so

\(H = (0.8)^{2} \times 40 \times 60 = 0.64 \times 2400 = 1536\) J,

which is the keyed option, 1536 J.

rows.stem: A cell of emf E is connected across an external resistance R. When current 'I' is drawn from the cell, the potential difference across the electrodes of the cell drops to V. The internal resistance 'r' of the cell is
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the expression alone: its table reads "4. ( d ) \(\left(\dfrac{E-V}{V}\right)R\)", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The terminal potential difference is the emf less the drop across the internal resistance:

\(V = E - Ir\), so \(r = \dfrac{E-V}{I}\).

The current is set by the external resistance, \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\), because \(V\) is the potential difference across \(R\). Substituting,

\(r = \dfrac{(E-V)R}{V} = \left(\dfrac{E-V}{V}\right)R\),

which is the keyed expression. The choice \(\dfrac{(E-V)R}{I}\) is the same algebra with \(I\) left in place of \(V/R\), and so is dimensionally wrong for a resistance.

rows.stem: Beams of electrons and protons move parallel to each other in the same direction. They

options.label: D
options.text: force of attraction or repulsion depends upon speed of beams.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "5. ( b ) Repel each other", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Take both beams to travel along \(+x\). The protons carry positive charge, so the proton beam is a conventional current along \(+x\). The electrons carry negative charge, so the electron beam is a conventional current along \(-x\).

The two beams are therefore equivalent to two ANTIPARALLEL currents, and antiparallel currents repel one another. So the beams repel, which is the keyed option.

The question is asking only about this magnetic interaction between the two equivalent currents; that is the discrimination it is built on, and it is why the electron-and-proton pairing is chosen rather than two electron beams (which would be parallel currents, and would attract).

rows.subtopic: Ampere's Circuital Law and the Solenoid
rows.stem: A long straight wire of radius 'a' carries a steady current 'I'. The current is uniformly distributed across its area of cross-section. The ratio of magnitude of magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}_1\) at \(\dfrac{a}{2}\) and \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}_2\) at distance 2a is
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "6. ( b ) 1", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Apply Ampere's circuital law to a circle of radius \(r\) coaxial with the wire.

Inside the wire \((r < a)\) only the fraction \(\dfrac{\pi r^{2}}{\pi a^{2}}\) of the current is enclosed, so \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^{2}}\). At \(r = \dfrac{a}{2}\),

\(B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a^{2}}\cdot\dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\).

Outside the wire the whole current is enclosed, so \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\). At \(r = 2a\),

\(B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (2a)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\).

The two are equal, so \(\dfrac{B_1}{B_2} = 1\), the keyed option. The point of the question is that \(B\) rises linearly out to the surface and then falls as \(1/r\), so a point at half the radius and a point at twice the radius happen to give the same field.

rows.stem: \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) and \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) represent the electric and the magnetic field of an electromagnetic wave respectively. The direction of propagation of the wave is along
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the expression alone: its table reads "7. ( c ) \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\)", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

In a plane electromagnetic wave \(\vec{E}\), \(\vec{B}\) and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular and form a right-handed set in that order. The wave therefore travels along \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\), which is the keyed option, and this is also the direction of the Poynting vector \(\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0}\,\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\) that carries the energy.

The choice \(\vec{B} \times \vec{E}\) points backwards along the propagation direction, since the cross product is anticommutative.

rows.stem: A ray of monochromatic light propagating in air, is incident on the surface of water. Which of the following will be the same for the reflected and refracted rays ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the word alone: its table reads "8. ( c ) Frequency", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The frequency of light is fixed by the source and is not altered by reflection or refraction, because the oscillating field at the boundary drives the medium on the far side at exactly the same rate. So the reflected and the refracted rays both have the frequency of the incident light, which is the keyed option.

The other three all differ. The speed in water is \(c/\mu\) but \(c\) for the reflected ray; the wavelength changes with the speed, since \(\lambda = v/\nu\); and the incident energy is shared between the two rays, so neither carries the same energy as the other.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: A beam of light travels from air into a medium. Its speed and wavelength in the medium are \(1.5 \times 10^8\) ms\(^{-1}\) and 230 nm respectively. The wavelength of light in air will be
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "9. ( c ) 460 nm", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The frequency is the same in both media, so \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda_{\text{air}}} = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_{\text{medium}}}\), giving

\(\lambda_{\text{air}} = \lambda_{\text{medium}} \times \dfrac{c}{v} = 230 \times \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{8}} = 230 \times 2 = 460\) nm.

That is the keyed option, 460 nm. Equivalently the refractive index is \(\mu = c/v = 2\), and the wavelength in a medium is \(\lambda_{\text{air}}/\mu\).

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem: Which one of the following metals does not exhibit emission of electrons from its surface when irradiated by visible light ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the name alone: its table reads "10. ( c ) Cadmium", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Visible light runs from about 400 nm to 700 nm, so its photons carry between about 1.8 eV and 3.1 eV. Photoemission occurs only if the photon energy exceeds the work function of the metal.

Caesium (about 2.14 eV), rubidium (about 2.16 eV) and sodium (about 2.75 eV) all have work functions inside or below that band, so visible light can eject electrons from them. Cadmium's work function is about 4.1 eV, well above the visible range, so visible photons cannot eject electrons from it and ultraviolet light is needed. Cadmium is therefore the keyed option.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: A hydrogen atom makes a transition from n = 5 to n = 1 orbit. The wavelength of photon emitted is \(\lambda\). The wavelength of photon emitted when it makes a transition from n = 5 to n = 2 orbit is
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "11. ( d ) \(\dfrac{32}{7}\lambda\)", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

For hydrogen, \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right)\).

For \(n = 5 \to 1\): \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = \dfrac{24R}{25}\).

For \(n = 5 \to 2\): \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda'} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = R\cdot\dfrac{25-4}{100} = \dfrac{21R}{100}\).

Dividing, \(\dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \dfrac{24R/25}{21R/100} = \dfrac{24}{25}\times\dfrac{100}{21} = \dfrac{2400}{525} = \dfrac{32}{7}\).

So \(\lambda' = \dfrac{32}{7}\lambda\), the keyed option. The longer wavelength is expected: the \(5 \to 2\) jump releases less energy than \(5 \to 1\).

rows.stem: The curve of binding energy per nucleon as a function of atomic mass number has a sharp peak for helium nucleus. This implies that helium nucleus is

options.label: D
options.text: more stable nucleus than its neighbours

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "12. ( d ) More stable nucleus than its neighbours.", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The binding energy per nucleon measures how tightly each nucleon is held. A sharp PEAK at helium-4 means its nucleons are bound more tightly than those of the nuclei on either side of it in mass number, so more energy per nucleon must be supplied to break it apart. That is exactly what it means to say the nucleus is more stable than its neighbours, which is the keyed option.

The other three read the curve backwards: a high binding energy per nucleon makes a nucleus harder, not easier, to break up, so helium-4 is neither unstable, nor radioactive, nor easily fissionable. (This peak is why alpha particles are emitted as a unit in alpha decay.)

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: In an extrinsic semiconductor, the number density of holes is \(4 \times 10^{20}\) m\(^{-3}\). If the number density of intrinsic carriers is \(1.2 \times 10^{15}\) m\(^{-3}\), the number density of electrons in it is
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the value alone: its table reads "13. ( c ) \(3.6 \times 10^{9}\) m\(^{-3}\)", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

In thermal equilibrium the law of mass action holds for any semiconductor, intrinsic or doped:

\(n_e n_h = n_i^{2}\).

So \(n_e = \dfrac{n_i^{2}}{n_h} = \dfrac{(1.2 \times 10^{15})^{2}}{4 \times 10^{20}} = \dfrac{1.44 \times 10^{30}}{4 \times 10^{20}} = 3.6 \times 10^{9}\) m\(^{-3}\).

That is the keyed option. The very small electron density beside a hole density of \(4 \times 10^{20}\) m\(^{-3}\) tells us this is a p-type semiconductor, in which the electrons are the minority carriers.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors
rows.stem: Pieces of copper and of silicon are initially at room temperature. Both are heated to temperature T. The conductivity of
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "14. ( d ) Copper decreases and silicon increases", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Copper is a metal. Its free-electron density does not change with temperature, but heating makes the lattice ions vibrate more violently, so collisions become more frequent, the relaxation time \(\tau\) falls, and since \(\sigma = \dfrac{n e^{2}\tau}{m}\) the conductivity DECREASES.

Silicon is a semiconductor. Heating breaks many more covalent bonds, so \(n\) rises roughly exponentially with temperature. That increase completely outweighs the fall in \(\tau\), so the conductivity INCREASES.

The combination "copper decreases and silicon increases" is therefore the keyed option, and the contrast is the standard way of telling a conductor from a semiconductor experimentally.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: The formation of depletion region in a p-n junction diode is due to

options.label: B
options.text: diffusion of both electrons and holes

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "15. ( b ) Diffusion of both electrons and holes.", and no working is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Immediately after the junction is formed there is a very large concentration gradient across it: electrons are plentiful on the n-side and holes on the p-side. Electrons therefore DIFFUSE from n to p and holes diffuse from p to n, and each recombines with a carrier of the opposite type near the junction.

That leaves behind the immobile ionised donors (positive) on the n-side and acceptors (negative) on the p-side. The thin layer so formed has almost no free carriers, and it is this that is called the depletion region. So the formation is due to the diffusion of both electrons and holes, which is the keyed option.

The dopant ATOMS themselves do not move; and drift is the reverse motion, driven by the field that the depletion region itself sets up, which is what eventually stops the diffusion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diamagnetic substances exhibit magnetism.
Reason (R) : Diamagnetic materials do not have permanent magnetic dipole moment.
rows.context: In question number 16 to 18, two statements are given - one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "16. ( b ) Both assertion (A) and Reason ( R ) are true and Reason( R) is not the correct explanation of assertion (A)", and no further justification is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The Assertion is TRUE. Diamagnetic substances do exhibit magnetism: placed in a magnetic field they acquire a weak magnetisation DIRECTED OPPOSITE to the field, so they are feebly repelled and tend to move from stronger to weaker parts of the field. Their relative permeability is slightly less than one and their susceptibility is small and negative.

The Reason is also TRUE. In a diamagnetic atom the electrons are all paired, so the orbital and spin magnetic moments cancel and the atom has no PERMANENT magnetic dipole moment.

But the Reason does not explain the Assertion. The absence of a permanent moment is what rules out para- and ferromagnetism; it says nothing about why any magnetism appears at all. The magnetism that diamagnetics DO show comes from a different cause, namely the moment INDUCED when the applied field alters the orbital motion of the electrons, which by Lenz's law opposes the field that produced it.

So both the Assertion and the Reason are true, while the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Work done in moving a charge around a closed path, in an electric field is always zero.
Reason (R) : Electrostatic force is a conservative force.
rows.context: In question number 16 to 18, two statements are given - one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "17. (a) Both Assertion (A) and Reason ( R) are true and Reason ( R) is the correct explanation of Assertion(A).", and no further justification is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The Assertion is TRUE. Moving a charge \(q\) from a point at potential \(V_1\) to a point at potential \(V_2\) needs work \(W = q(V_2 - V_1)\). On a closed path the start and end points coincide, so \(V_2 = V_1\) and \(W = 0\).

The Reason is also TRUE, and it is precisely why. The electrostatic force is conservative, which means the work it does depends only on the end points and not on the path; equivalently a potential energy function exists, and the work round any closed loop vanishes, \(\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0\).

So both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In Young's double slit experiment all fringes are of equal width.
Reason (R) : The fringe width depends upon wavelength of light (\(\lambda\)) used, distance of screen from plane of slits (D) and slits separation (d).
rows.context: In question number 16 to 18, two statements are given - one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter and the wording alone: its table reads "18. ( a ) Both Assertion ( A) and Reason ( R) are true and Reason (R ) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).", and no further justification is printed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The Assertion is TRUE. In Young's experiment the bright fringes lie at \(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\), so consecutive fringes are separated by \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\), the same for every \(n\). All the fringes therefore have the same width.

The Reason is also TRUE: the fringe width really does depend only on \(\lambda\), \(D\) and \(d\).

And the Reason explains the Assertion, because the content of the Reason is that the three quantities \(\lambda\), \(D\) and \(d\) are FIXED for a given set-up, while the order \(n\) does not appear in \(\beta\) at all. A quantity that does not depend on the fringe number must be the same for every fringe.

So both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem: Briefly explain why and how a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for WHY and 1 mark for HOW.

Why (the scheme's value points): because a galvanometer has very high sensitivity. Alternatively: it has a large resistance and would therefore change the value of the current in the circuit.

How (the scheme's value point): a galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter of the desired range by connecting a SHUNT of proper value ACROSS its coil.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme, to fill the two value points out:

A galvanometer gives full-scale deflection for a current of only a few microamperes, so the currents met in an ordinary circuit would drive it far past its scale. Its coil resistance is also comparatively large, and since an ammeter must be put in SERIES, inserting it would reduce the very current it was brought in to measure. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.

Both faults are cured by the same step: connect a small resistance \(S\) (the shunt) in parallel with the coil of resistance \(G\). The shunt carries most of the current and only a known small fraction passes through the coil, and the parallel combination \(\dfrac{GS}{G+S}\) is smaller than \(S\), so the meter barely disturbs the circuit.

If the galvanometer gives full-scale deflection for \(I_g\) and the ammeter is to read up to \(I\), the two parallel branches have equal potential difference:

\(I_g G = (I - I_g)S\), so \(S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g}\).

rows.stem: How are infrared waves produced ? Why are these waves referred to as heat waves ? Give any two uses of infrared waves.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 mark for the production, 1/2 for the reason they are called heat waves, and 1/2 + 1/2 for two uses.

Production (the scheme's value point): infrared waves are produced by HOT BODIES and by the VIBRATIONS OF MOLECULES.

Why they are called heat waves (the scheme's value point): because they are readily absorbed by water molecules, which increases their thermal energy and heats them.

Two uses (the scheme lists, and accepts any other relevant two): dehydration of fruits; the greenhouse effect; remote switches.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Infrared lies just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, roughly 700 nm to 1 mm in wavelength. Its photon energies match the vibrational and rotational energies of molecules, which is why molecules in a warm body radiate it and why molecules in an absorber take it up so readily. The energy absorbed goes straight into molecular vibration, that is, into internal energy, so the absorber warms up and the radiation earns the name heat wave.

Other acceptable uses: infrared remote controls for televisions and other appliances; physiotherapy for treating muscular pain; infrared detectors and night-vision or thermal imaging; long-distance photography through haze, since infrared is scattered less than visible light.

rows.stem: How are X-rays produced ? Give any two uses of these.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the production and 1/2 + 1/2 for two uses.

Production (the scheme's value point): when FAST MOVING ELECTRONS STRIKE A HEAVY TARGET LIKE TUNGSTEN, X-rays are produced.

Two uses (the scheme lists, and accepts any two of these or other correct uses): as a diagnostic tool in medicine; treatment for certain forms of cancer; to study crystal structure.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

In an X-ray tube electrons emitted from a hot cathode are accelerated through a large potential difference, a few tens of kilovolts, and strike a heavy metal anode such as tungsten or molybdenum. Their sudden deceleration in the strong fields of the target nuclei radiates a continuous X-ray spectrum, and the knocking out of inner-shell electrons adds the sharp characteristic lines.

Their usefulness rests on their very short wavelength, about \(10^{-8}\) m down to \(10^{-13}\) m. That is why they penetrate flesh but are stopped by bone, giving a radiograph; why they can be focused on a tumour to kill malignant tissue in radiotherapy; and why, being comparable with interatomic spacings, they are diffracted by crystals and so reveal crystal structure.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: In the given figure the radius of curvature of curved face in the plano-convex and the plano-concave lens is 15 cm each. The refractive index of the material of the lenses is 1.5. Find the final position of the image formed.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem says 'in the given figure' and supplies neither the arrangement nor the separation. The drawing shows three parallel rays entering from the left, a plano-convex lens, then a plano-concave lens, with a dimension arrow marked '20 cm' beneath them. That 20 cm and the order/orientation of the two lenses exist ONLY in the figure, so the question is unanswerable without it. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots the full 2 marks for finding the final position of the image, in four steps.

Step 1, the two focal lengths, from \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\):

for the plano-convex lens, \(\dfrac{1}{f_1} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = \dfrac{0.5}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30}\), so \(f_1 = +30\) cm;

for the plano-concave lens the curved face bends the light the other way, so \(f_2 = -30\) cm.

Step 2: the incident rays are PARALLEL to the axis, that is, the object is at infinity, so the first lens forms a real image at its own focus, \(v_1 = +30\) cm from the plano-convex lens.

Step 3: the two lenses are 20 cm apart (this separation is marked only on the figure), so that image lies \(30 - 20 = 10\) cm BEYOND the second lens. The light is intercepted before it gets there, so for the plano-concave lens it is a VIRTUAL OBJECT and \(u_2 = +10\) cm.

Step 4, the lens equation for the second lens, \(\dfrac{1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{u_2}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{10}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{3-1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{15}\)

\(v_2 = +15\) cm.

The final image is real and is formed 15 cm from the plano-concave lens, on the far side from the incoming light.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the positive sign of \(u_2\) is the whole trick of the question. The Cartesian convention takes distances measured in the direction of the incident light as positive, and here the converging beam is heading towards a point 10 cm PAST the lens, so \(u_2\) is positive rather than the usual negative. Note also that the lenses cannot be treated as a combination in contact, because they are 20 cm apart.

rows.stem:
What happens to the interference pattern when two coherent sources are
(a) infinitely close, and
(b) far apart from each other
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for each part.

(a) When \(d\) is very small, since \(\beta \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\), the fringe width \(\beta\) will be very large and a single patch will occupy the whole field of view, so the pattern cannot be observed. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a candidate simply writes that the fringe width will increase, or that the fringes will not be observed.

(b) When the sources are far apart, that is \(d\) is very large, the fringe width will be so small that the fringes are not resolved and cannot be seen separately. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given for writing that the fringe width will decrease, or that the fringes may not be observed.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: both halves follow from the single relation \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\), and the two failures are opposite ends of the same problem. Bringing the sources together stretches one fringe until it is wider than the screen, so there is nothing to compare it against; pushing them apart squeezes the fringes below what the eye or the detector can separate, so they blur into uniform illumination. In both cases the interference is still happening; it is only the OBSERVATION of a pattern that fails.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: What is meant by ionisation energy ? Write its value for hydrogen atom.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the meaning and 1 mark for the value.

Meaning (the scheme's value point): ionisation energy is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from an isolated atom of an element. The scheme's stated alternative: it is the energy required to excite an electron from the energy level \(n = 1\) to \(n = \infty\) in an isolated atom.

Value (the scheme's value point): the ionisation energy for the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

In the Bohr model the energy of the \(n\)th level of hydrogen is \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\) eV, so the ground state sits at \(E_1 = -13.6\) eV. Ionisation means lifting the electron to \(n = \infty\), where \(E_\infty = 0\), so the energy needed is

\(E_\infty - E_1 = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6\) eV.

The word ISOLATED matters: the atom must not be bound in a molecule or a solid, and it must start in its ground state, otherwise a smaller energy would suffice.

rows.stem: Define the term, mass defect. How is it related to stability of the nucleus ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the definition and 1 mark for the relation with stability.

Definition (the scheme's value point): mass defect is the difference between the actual mass of the nucleus and the sum of the masses of its nucleons.

Relation with stability (the scheme's value point): the greater the mass defect, the greater the binding energy and the more stable the nucleus. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given for writing that the mass defect is proportional to the stability of the nucleus.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The mass defect is defined as a POSITIVE quantity, the amount by which the separated nucleons weigh MORE than the nucleus they make:

\(\Delta M = \left[Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n\right] - M_{\text{nucleus}}\).

(The marking scheme names the same two quantities in the opposite order. Take the ordering above, since it is the one that makes the scheme's own next line true: only a positive \(\Delta M\) gives a positive binding energy.)

The missing mass appears as the energy released when the nucleus is assembled, \(E_b = \Delta M\,c^{2}\), and this is exactly the energy that must be supplied to pull the nucleus apart again. A larger mass defect therefore means a larger binding energy.

One refinement worth knowing: what measures stability from nucleus to nucleus is the binding energy PER NUCLEON, not the total. Uranium has a far larger mass defect than iron yet is less stable, because its binding energy is shared among many more nucleons.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: Draw energy band diagram for an n-type and p-type semiconductor at T > 0 K.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for each diagram and answers this question entirely with two drawings, reproduced from NCERT and captioned "(a) n-type semiconductor" and "(b) p-type semiconductor", both at \(T > 0\) K. No prose is printed.

What the two diagrams show, described here so the answer can be used from text:

n-type. Draw the valence band \(E_V\) at the bottom and the conduction band \(E_C\) above it, separated by the forbidden gap \(E_g\). Mark a dashed DONOR level \(E_D\) lying just BELOW \(E_C\), a gap of only about 0.01 eV. At \(T > 0\) K that gap is far smaller than \(E_g\), so almost every donor electron has already been lifted into the conduction band: show a large number of electrons (filled circles) spread through the conduction band, and only the few electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band that thermal breaking of the bonds itself produces.

p-type. Draw the same two bands and gap, but mark a dashed ACCEPTOR level \(E_A\) lying just ABOVE \(E_V\), a gap of about 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV. At \(T > 0\) K electrons are easily excited from the valence band into \(E_A\), so show a large number of holes (open circles) left behind in the valence band, and only a few thermally generated electrons in the conduction band.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the single idea both pictures carry is that the dopant level sits within a few hundredths of an electron-volt of the nearby band, against a gap \(E_g\) of about 1.1 eV in silicon, so at room temperature the dopants are essentially all ionised while the host lattice is barely ionised at all. That is why a tiny dopant fraction can raise the conductivity by orders of magnitude, and why the majority carriers are electrons in n-type and holes in p-type material.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem:
Answer the following giving reasons :
(i) A p-n junction diode is damaged by a strong current.
(ii) Impurities are added in intrinsic semiconductors.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for each reason.

(i) (the scheme's value point) Due to a strong current, a junction diode gets heated; consequently a large number of covalent bonds are broken and the junction is damaged.

(ii) (the scheme's value point) The deliberate addition of impurity atoms to an intrinsic semiconductor increases its conductivity and makes it suitable for making electronic devices. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a student writes that no electronic device can be developed using an intrinsic semiconductor because of its low conductivity.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

(i) The power dissipated at the junction is \(I^{2}R\), so it rises as the SQUARE of the current. The heat is produced in the very thin depletion layer, where it cannot be carried away quickly, so the local temperature climbs sharply. The broken covalent bonds flood the region with carriers, which lets even more current through and produces still more heat. This runaway ends in permanent damage to the junction, and the diode no longer rectifies.

(ii) A pure semiconductor at room temperature has an extremely small carrier concentration, of the order of \(10^{16}\) m\(^{-3}\) in silicon, so its conductivity is far too low to be useful. Doping with a pentavalent or a trivalent impurity raises the carrier density by many orders of magnitude, and, just as importantly, it lets us CHOOSE which carrier is in the majority. Making one piece n-type and another p-type is what gives the junction on which every diode and transistor depends.

rows.stem: Two charged conducting spheres of radii a and b are connected to each other by a wire. Find the ratio of the electric fields at their surfaces.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots the full 3 marks for finding the ratio of the electric fields at the surfaces.

Step 1 (the scheme's value point): when connected by a conducting wire both spheres will be at the same potential.

\(k\dfrac{q_1}{a} = k\dfrac{q_2}{b}\), so \(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2} = \dfrac{a}{b}\).

Step 2: the field just outside the surface of a charged conducting sphere of radius \(R\) carrying charge \(q\) is \(E = k\dfrac{q}{R^{2}}\), so

\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{k\,q_1/a^{2}}{k\,q_2/b^{2}} = \dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\cdot\dfrac{b^{2}}{a^{2}} = \dfrac{a}{b}\cdot\dfrac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}\)

\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{b}{a}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the wire makes the two spheres one conductor, and a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential, which is the only physical input the problem needs. Writing the result as \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\) with \(\sigma\) the surface charge density shows what it means: the SMALLER sphere ends up with the smaller charge but the larger surface density, and so the stronger field at its surface. The same fact, pushed to a sharp point where the radius of curvature is tiny, is what produces corona discharge and is the principle of the lightning conductor.

rows.stem:
A parallel plate capacitor (A) of capacitance C is charged by a battery to voltage V. The battery is disconnected and an uncharged capacitor (B) of capacitance 2C is connected across A. Find the ratio of
(i) final charges on A and B.
(ii) total electrostatic energy stored in A and B finally and that stored in A initially.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 + 1/2 marks for the ratio of the final charges and 1 + 1 for the energy ratio.

(i) Initially \(Q = CV\) on capacitor A. When B is connected across A the two are in parallel and so end at a common potential \(V_1\), giving \(q_A = C_A V_1\) and \(q_B = C_B V_1\). Hence

\(\dfrac{q_A}{q_B} = \dfrac{C_A}{C_B} = \dfrac{C}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

(ii) Charge is conserved, \(q_A + q_B = Q\), so with the ratio above \(q_A = \dfrac{Q}{3}\) and \(q_B = \dfrac{2Q}{3}\).

\(\dfrac{U_f}{U_i} = \dfrac{\dfrac{q_A^{2}}{2C_A} + \dfrac{q_B^{2}}{2C_B}}{\dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C_A}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{(Q/3)^{2}}{2C} + \dfrac{(2Q/3)^{2}}{4C}}{\dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{Q^{2}}{18C} + \dfrac{Q^{2}}{9C}}{\dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}} = \dfrac{Q^{2}/6C}{Q^{2}/2C} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

The scheme also prints the shorter route: the common potential is \(V_1 = \dfrac{Q_1 + Q_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \dfrac{Q}{3C} = \dfrac{V}{3}\), so

\(\dfrac{U_f}{U_i} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}C_{eq}V_1^{2}}{\tfrac{1}{2}C_A V^{2}} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}(3C)\left(\dfrac{V}{3}\right)^{2}}{\tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: two-thirds of the stored energy has disappeared, and this is not a mistake. The battery has been disconnected, so no energy comes in; the loss is dissipated as heat in the connecting wires (and as electromagnetic radiation) while the charge redistributes. The loss occurs however small the resistance of the wires is, which is the point the question is built around.

rows.stem: Define current density and relaxation time. Derive an expression for resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of charge carriers in the conductor and relaxation time.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 mark for each definition and 2 marks for the derivation.

Current density (the scheme's value point): the current flowing per unit area of cross-section of a conductor. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a candidate simply writes \(j = \dfrac{I}{A}\).

Relaxation time (the scheme's value point): the average time interval between two successive collisions for the drifting electrons in a conductor.

Derivation, following the scheme's steps:

\(I = nAev_d\), but \(v_d = \dfrac{eE}{m}\tau\), so \(I = nAe\cdot\dfrac{eE}{m}\tau\).

\(j = \dfrac{I}{A} = \dfrac{ne^{2}E\tau}{m}\).

But \(j = \dfrac{E}{\rho}\), therefore

\(\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the drift velocity itself comes from the free-electron picture. Between collisions an electron is accelerated by the field with \(a = \dfrac{eE}{m}\), and each collision destroys the memory of the previous one, so the velocity it has picked up on average when the next collision occurs is \(a\tau = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\). The result \(\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\) is worth reading as the answer to Q14 above: resistivity depends on the material only through \(n\) and \(\tau\), and heating a metal shortens \(\tau\) while heating a semiconductor raises \(n\).

rows.stem:
A series CR circuit with R = 200 \(\Omega\) and C = \((50/\pi)\) \(\mu\)F is connected across an ac source of peak voltage \(\varepsilon_0\) = 100 V and frequency \(\nu\) = 50 Hz. Calculate
(a) impedance of the circuit (Z), (b) phase angle \((\phi)\), and (c) voltage across the resistor.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark to each of the three parts.

(a) \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_C^{2}}\), with \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C}\).

\(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2 \times \pi \times 50 \times \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 200\,\Omega\)

(the \(\pi\) in the capacitance cancels the \(\pi\) in \(2\pi\nu\), which is why the odd-looking value of \(C\) was chosen).

\(Z = \sqrt{(200)^{2} + (200)^{2}} = 200\sqrt{2}\,\Omega \approx 283\,\Omega\) (the marking scheme prints this as \(\approx 282\,\Omega\)).

(b) \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_C}{R} = \dfrac{200}{200} = 1\), so \(\phi = 45^{\circ}\) or \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) rad.

(c) \(V_{rms} \text{ across } R = I_{rms}R = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}R = \dfrac{100/\sqrt{2}}{200\sqrt{2}} \times 200 = 50\) V.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the peak source voltage of 100 V is turned into an rms value by dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\), which is why \(100/\sqrt{2}\) appears in part (c) and not 100. The answer is exact, because the two \(\sqrt{2}\) factors cancel. In a CR circuit the current LEADS the source voltage, so the phase angle of \(45^{\circ}\) is a lead. Worth checking: the voltage across the capacitor is also \(I_{rms}X_C = 50\) V, and \(\sqrt{50^{2} + 50^{2}} = 50\sqrt{2} \approx 70.7\) V is the rms source voltage, as it must be, since the two voltages are \(90^{\circ}\) out of phase and add as vectors rather than arithmetically.

rows.stem: Define critical angle for a given pair of media and total internal reflection. Obtain the relation between the critical angle and refractive index of the medium.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for each definition and 1 mark for the relation.

Critical angle (the scheme's value point): when a ray of light passes from a denser to a rarer medium, the value of the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction becomes \(90^{\circ}\) is called the critical angle for that pair of media.

Total internal reflection (the scheme's value point): when a ray of light passes from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle for that pair of media, the ray undergoes reflection. This is called total internal reflection.

Relation, following the scheme: from Snell's law at the denser-to-rarer boundary, and putting the angle of incidence equal to the critical angle \(i_c\) so that the angle of refraction is \(90^{\circ}\),

\(\mu \sin i_c = 1 \times \sin 90^{\circ} = 1\)

\(\mu = \dfrac{1}{\sin i_c}\),

where \(\mu\) is the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer one.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: two conditions are needed together, and the definitions above contain both. Light must be going from denser to rarer, so that the refracted ray bends AWAY from the normal and can reach \(90^{\circ}\) at all; and the angle of incidence must exceed \(i_c\), beyond which \(\sin r\) would have to exceed one, so no refracted ray is possible and the whole of the light is reflected back. The word TOTAL is exact: unlike ordinary reflection at a surface, no fraction of the energy is transmitted. The relation also says that the denser the medium, the smaller its critical angle: for water \(\mu = 1.33\) gives about \(49^{\circ}\), for ordinary glass \(\mu = 1.5\) gives about \(42^{\circ}\), which is why a \(45^{\circ}\) prism turns light through a right angle.

rows.stem:
(i) Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion giving an example of each.
(ii) Explain the release of energy in nuclear fission and fusion on the basis of binding energy per nucleon curve.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the difference, 1/2 + 1/2 for the examples, and 1/2 + 1/2 for the explanation from the binding-energy curve.

[CBSE marking scheme: its second fusion example is printed as \(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow ^{3}_{2}\mathrm{H} + n + Q_2\). The product carries atomic number 2, which is HELIUM, so the symbol should read \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\); this is the helium-3 branch of the deuterium-deuterium reaction, and NCERT prints it with He. The mass and charge numbers balance correctly either way, so only the chemical symbol is wrong, and it is corrected below.]

(i) Nuclear fission (the scheme's value point): a process in which a heavy nucleus, when excited (say on being bombarded by a slow moving neutron), splits into two lighter nuclei of nearly comparable masses with the release of a large amount of energy.

Example of fission:

\(^{1}_{0}n + ^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow ^{236}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow ^{144}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + ^{89}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}n + Q\)

Nuclear fusion (the scheme's value point): a process in which two lighter nuclei fuse, at extremely high temperature, to form a heavier nucleus, with a large amount of energy released.

Examples of fusion (the scheme prints these three and accepts any other correct reaction):

\(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow ^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + e^{+} + \nu + Q_1\)

\(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow ^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + n + Q_2\)

\(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow ^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + Q_3\)

(ii) The scheme's value point: the binding energy per nucleon of the PRODUCTS of these nuclear reactions, both fission and fusion, is greater than that of the reactants.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme, to say why that releases energy: the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve rises steeply from hydrogen to a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV near iron (mass number about 56) and then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV at mass number 238. Moving nucleons UP that curve means they end more tightly bound, and the extra binding energy is released. A heavy nucleus can climb the curve by SPLITTING into two middle-mass fragments, which is fission; two very light nuclei can climb it by JOINING, which is fusion. The energy released in each case is \((\text{total BE of products}) - (\text{total BE of reactants})\), equivalently \(\Delta M\,c^{2}\) for the reaction. Both processes are thus the same idea applied at the two ends of one curve.

rows.stem:
(i) How is the size of a nucleus found experimentally ? Write the relation between the radius and mass number of a nucleus.
(ii) Prove that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 mark for the experimental determination, 1 mark for the relation, and 1 1/2 marks for the proof.

(i) The scheme's value point: the size of the nucleus of an atom is determined by SCATTERING EXPERIMENTS, in which fast electrons are used to bombard targets.

Relation between radius and mass number:

\(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\)

(ii) Density of the nucleus, following the scheme:

\(\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{m \times A}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(R_0 A^{1/3}\right)^{3}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^{3} A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^{3}}\)

The mass number \(A\) has cancelled, so the density of the nucleus is independent of \(A\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: \(R_0\) is a constant, about \(1.2 \times 10^{-15}\) m, and \(m\) is the average mass of one nucleon. Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment first established that the nucleus exists and set an upper bound on its size from the distance of closest approach; the accurate sizes of nuclei across the periodic table came later from scattering FAST ELECTRONS off them, which is what the scheme's value point refers to and what NCERT states.

The cancellation of \(A\) is the whole content of part (ii): since \(R \propto A^{1/3}\), the volume goes as \(A\), and the mass also goes as \(A\), so the ratio is the same for every nucleus. Putting the numbers in gives about \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\) kg m\(^{-3}\), some \(10^{14}\) times the density of ordinary matter. It also says that nuclear matter is INCOMPRESSIBLE and that nucleons are packed at a fixed spacing, which is one of the facts the liquid-drop model is built on.

rows.stem:
(i) Use Gauss' law to obtain an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long thin straight wire with uniform linear charge density \(\lambda\).
(ii) An infinitely long positively charged straight wire has a linear charge density \(\lambda\). An electron is revolving in a circle with a constant speed \(v\) such that the wire passes through the centre, and is perpendicular to the plane, of the circle. Find the kinetic energy of the electron in terms of magnitudes of its charge and linear charge density \(\lambda\) on the wire.
(iii) Draw a graph of kinetic energy as a function of linear charge density \(\lambda\).
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 2 marks for the derivation, 2 marks for the kinetic energy and 1 mark for the graph.

(i) The scheme's derivation, with its diagram of a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius \(r\) and length \(l\) drawn coaxially around the charged wire:

Flux through the Gaussian surface, \(\phi = E\,(2\pi r l)\).

According to Gauss's law, \(E\,(2\pi r l) = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\), and the charge enclosed is \(q = \lambda l\), so

\(E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

(ii) The scheme's working, with its sketch of the electron on a circle threaded by the wire:

the electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force, \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = eE\),

so kinetic energy \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}eEr = \dfrac{1}{2}e\cdot\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\cdot r\)

\(K = \dfrac{e\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\)

(iii) Since \(K \propto \lambda\), the graph is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN, with \(K\) on the vertical axis and \(\lambda\) on the horizontal axis, of slope \(\dfrac{e}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\). The scheme prints exactly this: a straight line rising from the origin, labelled \(K\) up the vertical axis and \(\lambda\) along the horizontal.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

On the derivation in (i): only the CURVED face of the cylinder contributes to the flux. By symmetry the field of an infinite line of charge is radial and its magnitude depends only on \(r\), so it is parallel to the two flat end faces and their flux is zero, and it is constant over the curved face so the integral is just \(E\) times its area \(2\pi r l\). The length \(l\) then cancels, which it must, since the answer cannot depend on how long a Gaussian surface we chose to draw.

On the result in (ii): notice that \(r\) has cancelled. The kinetic energy of the electron does not depend on the radius of its orbit at all, and neither therefore does its speed. That is peculiar to the \(1/r\) field of a line charge: the centripetal requirement \(mv^{2}/r\) falls off at exactly the same rate as the attractive force, so every circular orbit is traversed at the same speed. It is also why the answer can be written purely in terms of \(e\) and \(\lambda\), as the question asks.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem:
(i) Consider two identical point charges located at points (0, 0) and (a, 0).
(1) Is there a point on the line joining them at which the electric field is zero ?
(2) Is there a point on the line joining them at which the electric potential is zero ?
Justify your answers for each case.
(ii) State the significance of negative value of electrostatic potential energy of a system of charges.
Three charges are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle ABC of side 2.0 m as shown in figure. Calculate the electric potential energy of the system of three charges.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - part (ii) says 'as shown in figure' and the stem states only the side length. The drawing is an equilateral triangle with vertex A at the top and B (left) and C (right) at the base, each corner a small open circle, and the three charge values written beside them. Those three values are the only data for the calculation and appear nowhere in the text. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 2 marks for part (i), 1 mark for the significance and 2 marks for the calculation.

(i) The scheme's value points:

(1) YES, the electric field is zero at the mid point. The electric field is a vector quantity, and here its resultant is zero.

(2) NO, the potential cannot be zero on the line joining the charges. The electric potential is a scalar quantity, and the net potential due to two IDENTICAL charges cannot be zero.

(ii) The scheme's value point on significance: a negative value of the electrostatic potential energy of a system signifies that the system has ATTRACTIVE forces. The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a candidate writes that the system is stable, or bound.

Calculation, following the scheme, with the three charges read off the figure as \(q_A = +4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}\), \(q_B = -4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}\), \(q_C = +2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}\) and every side \(r = 2.0\) m:

\(U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q_A q_B}{r} + \dfrac{q_B q_C}{r} + \dfrac{q_C q_A}{r}\right]\)

\(U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9}}{2}\left[(4)(-4) + (-4)(2) + (2)(4)\right] \times 10^{-12}\)

\(U = 4.5 \times 10^{9} \times (-16 - 8 + 8) \times 10^{-12} = 4.5 \times 10^{9} \times (-16) \times 10^{-12}\)

\(U = -7.2 \times 10^{-2}\) J

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

On (i)(1): at the mid point the two charges are equidistant, so the two field vectors have equal magnitudes; being on opposite sides they point in opposite directions along the line, so they cancel exactly. That is the only point on the line where this happens, since anywhere else the nearer charge wins.

On (i)(2): a potential is a sum of scalars, \(V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)\), and both terms carry the SAME sign because the charges are identical. A sum of two terms of the same sign, neither of which can vanish at a finite point, cannot be zero. Had the charges been equal and OPPOSITE, the answers would have been the other way round: the potential would vanish at the mid point and the field would vanish nowhere on the segment between them. That contrast is what the question is built on.

On (ii): the potential energy is the work an outside agent must do to assemble the charges from infinity. A negative value means the assembly RELEASED energy, so positive work must now be done to pull the charges back to infinity, which is exactly what is meant by calling the system bound. Note that the pair \(q_B q_C\) and the pair \(q_C q_A\) here contribute \(-8\) and \(+8\) and cancel, so the whole of the answer comes from the strongly attractive \(+4\,\mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(-4\,\mu\mathrm{C}\) pair.

rows.stem:
(i) Define coefficient of self-induction. Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length \(l\), area of cross-section A having N turns.
(ii) Calculate the self-inductance of a coil using the following data obtained when an AC source of frequency \(\left(\dfrac{200}{\pi}\right)\) Hz and a DC source is applied across the coil.

AC Source

| S.No. | V (Volts) | I (A) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.0 | 0.5 |
| 2 | 6.0 | 1.0 |
| 3 | 9.0 | 1.5 |

DC Source

| S.No. | V (Volts) | I (A) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4.0 | 1.0 |
| 2 | 6.0 | 1.5 |
| 3 | 8.0 | 2.0 |
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the definition, 2 marks for the derivation and 2 marks for the calculation.

(i) Definition (the scheme's value point): the coefficient of self-induction is the amount of magnetic flux associated with a coil when unit current flows through it. The scheme's stated alternative: it is the magnitude of the emf induced in a coil when the current through it changes at the rate of 1 A/s.

Derivation, following the scheme:

the magnetic field due to a current \(I\) flowing in the solenoid is \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{l}\);

the total magnetic flux linked with the solenoid is \(N\phi_B = (N)\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{l}\right)(A) = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} I A}{l}\);

the self-inductance is \(L = \dfrac{N\phi_B}{I}\), so

\(L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} A}{l}\)

(ii) Calculation, following the scheme. From the tables, the AC source gives the IMPEDANCE and the DC source gives the RESISTANCE:

\(Z = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{3.0}{0.5} = \dfrac{6.0}{1.0} = \dfrac{9.0}{1.5} = 6\,\Omega\); \(R = \dfrac{4.0}{1.0} = \dfrac{6.0}{1.5} = \dfrac{8.0}{2.0} = 4\,\Omega\)

\(Z^{2} = R^{2} + X_L^{2}\), so \(X_L^{2} = Z^{2} - R^{2} = 36 - 16 = 20\) and \(X_L = 2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.5\,\Omega\)

\(2\pi\nu L = 4.5\), so \(L = \dfrac{4.5}{2 \times \pi \times \dfrac{200}{\pi}} = \dfrac{4.5}{400}\)

\(L = 1.1 \times 10^{-2}\) H \(= 11\) mH

The scheme adds a note: do not deduct marks if a student writes the answer as \(0.5\sqrt{5} \times 10^{-2}\) H, which is the same quantity kept in surd form, \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{400} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{200} = 1.118 \times 10^{-2}\) H.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the whole method rests on the fact that an inductor offers reactance only to an ALTERNATING current. To direct current, once the current has become steady, \(\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 0\) and the coil behaves as its resistance alone, so the DC table gives \(R\). With alternating current the same coil offers \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}}\), so subtracting in quadrature isolates \(X_L\). Three readings are given in each table only so that the student can check that \(V/I\) really is constant, that is, that the coil is ohmic and the readings are consistent. The awkward frequency \(\dfrac{200}{\pi}\) Hz is chosen so that \(2\pi\nu = 400\) exactly and the \(\pi\) disappears.

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the principle and working of an ac generator. Hence, obtain an expression for the instantaneous value of the emf generated.
(ii) The coil of an ac generator consists of 100 turns of wire, each of area 0.5 m\(^2\). The resistance of the wire is 100 \(\Omega\). The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of 0.8 T perpendicular to its axis of rotation, at a constant angular speed of 60 radian per second. Calculate the maximum emf generated and power dissipated in the coil.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the labelled diagram, 1/2 for the principle, 1/2 for the working, 1 for the expression, and 1 + 1 for the two calculations.

(i) The diagram (the scheme reproduces the NCERT figure): a rectangular COIL mounted on an AXLE, free to rotate between the pole pieces marked N and S of a magnet; the two ends of the coil are brought out to two SLIP RINGS, which turn with the coil and press against two fixed CARBON BRUSHES, and the alternating emf is taken from the brushes to the external circuit.

Principle (the scheme's value point): it is based on the principle of ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION. Whenever there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with a coil, an emf is induced in the coil.

Working (the scheme's value point): when a rectangular coil is rotated in a magnetic field, the magnetic flux changes continuously, which induces an emf, and the direction of the current changes periodically.

Expression, following the scheme. With the coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) rotating at angular speed \(\omega\) in a field \(B\), the flux linked with each turn is \(\phi = BA\cos\omega t\), so

\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{-N\,d\phi}{dt} = -NBA\dfrac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)\)

\(\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t\)

(ii) The peak emf is \(\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega\), so

\(\varepsilon_0 = 100 \times 0.8 \times 0.5 \times 60 = 2400\) V

Power dissipated, \(P = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{rms}^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2400}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}}{100} = \dfrac{2400^{2}}{2 \times 100} = \dfrac{5760000}{200} = 28800\) W \(= 28.8\) kW

The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a candidate calculates the power using \(\varepsilon_{rms} I_{rms}\) or \(I_{rms}^{2}R\) instead.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the minus sign in Faraday's law is Lenz's law, and it disappears from the final expression only because differentiating \(\cos\omega t\) brings out a second minus. The emf is a maximum when \(\sin\omega t = 1\), that is when the plane of the coil is PARALLEL to the field, because that is the position in which the flux, though momentarily zero, is changing fastest. The three alternative power formulae agree because the circuit named here is purely resistive: \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{rms}}{R} = \dfrac{2400}{100\sqrt{2}} = 12\sqrt{2} \approx 17.0\) A, and \(I_{rms}^{2}R = 288 \times 100 = 28.8\) kW as before.

rows.stem:
(i) State Huygen's principle. With the help of a diagram, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection.
(ii) A concave mirror of focal length 12 cm forms a three times magnified virtual image of an object. Find the distance of the object from the mirror.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the statement, 1 for the diagram, 1 for the verification and 2 for the calculation.

(i) Huygens's principle (the scheme's value point): each point of the wavefront is the source of a secondary disturbance, and the wavelets emanating from these points spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave. These wavelets emanating from the wavefront are usually referred to as secondary wavelets, and a common tangent to all these spheres gives the new position of the wavefront at a later time.

The diagram the scheme prints: a reflecting surface MN drawn as a hatched line; a plane INCIDENT WAVEFRONT arriving obliquely and meeting the surface at A, with the wave reaching C further along the surface; the angle of incidence \(i\) marked at A and the angle of reflection \(r\) marked at C; and the plane REFLECTED WAVEFRONT leaving as the tangent from C to the secondary wavelet centred on A, with E the point of tangency and the right angles at E and at B marked.

Verification of the law of reflection, following the scheme's congruence:

In \(\triangle AEC\) and \(\triangle CBA\):

\(EC = AB\) (each equal to \(c \times t\), the distance the wave travels in the same time \(t\));

\(\angle AEC = \angle CBA\) (\(90^{\circ}\) each, since a wavefront is perpendicular to the direction of travel);

\(AC = AC\) (common side).

By RHS congruency, \(\triangle AEC \cong \triangle CBA\), and therefore \(\angle i = \angle r\).

(ii) The scheme's working. A virtual, magnified image in a concave mirror is ERECT, so \(m = +3\), and \(f = -12\) cm:

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = 3\), so \(v = -3u\).

Using the mirror formula \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{-3u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-12}\)

\(\dfrac{-1 + 3}{3u} = \dfrac{-1}{12}\), so \(\dfrac{2}{3u} = \dfrac{-1}{12}\) and \(3u = -24\)

\(u = -8\) cm

The object is 8 cm in front of the mirror.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the sign of \(m\) is the step that decides the whole problem. "Virtual" fixes the image as erect for a mirror, so \(m\) is \(+3\) and not \(-3\); taking it negative would put the object at \(u = -16\) cm, outside the focus, where a concave mirror forms a REAL inverted image, contradicting the question. The answer also passes the standard check: a concave mirror gives a virtual magnified image only when the object lies between the pole and the focus, and 8 cm is indeed inside the focal length of 12 cm.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a labelled ray diagram showing the image formation by a refracting telescope. Define its magnifying power. Write two limitations of a refracting telescope over a reflecting telescope.
(ii) The focal lengths of the objective and the eye-piece of a compound microscope are 1.0 cm and 2.5 cm respectively. Find the tube length of the microscope for obtaining a magnification of 300.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 1/2 marks for the labelled diagram, 1 for the definition, 1/2 + 1/2 for two limitations and 1 1/2 for the calculation.

(i) The diagram (the scheme reproduces the standard NCERT figure): parallel rays from a distant object arriving at the OBJECTIVE, a large lens of long focal length \(f_o\); they converge to a real, inverted image at the focus of the objective, of height \(h\), marked at \(A\)/\(B'\); the EYEPIECE, a small lens of short focal length \(f_e\), is placed so that this image lies at its focus, and the rays leave it parallel to give a final image at infinity; the angle \(\alpha\) subtended at the objective and the angle \(\beta\) subtended at the eye are marked, with the eye drawn at the right. The scheme notes that half a mark is to be deducted if a student does not show the DIRECTION OF PROPAGATION of the light, and that full credit is also to be given for a ray diagram drawn for the final image at the near point.

Definition of magnifying power (the scheme's value point): it is the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle subtended by the object at the lens or at the eye. For the normal adjustment this gives \(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\).

Two limitations of a refracting telescope over a reflecting telescope (the scheme lists five and asks for any two): less resolving power; difficult mechanical support; less bright image; it suffers from chromatic aberration; the image suffers from spherical aberration.

(ii) The scheme's working, with \(f_o = 1.0\) cm, \(f_e = 2.5\) cm, \(m = 300\) and \(D = 25\) cm:

\(|m| = \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}\)

\(300 = \dfrac{L}{1.0}\cdot\dfrac{25}{2.5} = 10\,L\)

\(L = 30\) cm

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

On the limitations: they follow from one fact, that a refractor must use a LENS as its objective while a reflector uses a mirror. Light passes THROUGH a lens, so different colours are brought to different foci and chromatic aberration is unavoidable; a mirror reflects all colours alike and has none. A large lens can only be supported at its rim and sags under its own weight, whereas a mirror can be supported over its whole back, which is why the largest objectives are all mirrors, and why a refractor's smaller aperture gives it both a dimmer image and a poorer resolving power, since the resolving limit is \(\dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D}\).

On the calculation: the formula used is the standard approximation for a compound microscope in which the final image is at the near point, with the TUBE LENGTH \(L\) taken as the distance between the two lenses and used in place of the image distance from the objective. It is accurate when both focal lengths are small compared with \(L\), which they are here.

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem: Explain the reason of jumping of the ring when the switch is closed in the circuit.
rows.context:
Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off.

Answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the passage never mentions a switch or a battery, yet sub-parts (i) and (ii) both turn on them. The drawing labels 'Copper Ring (free to move)' sitting on a vertical 'Iron Core', a 'Coil' wound round the lower cylinder, a 'Switch' and a 'Battery' with its + and - terminals marked, wired in one loop with the coil. Describing the battery polarity or the sense of the winding is deliberately withheld - that is the directed quantity the answer turns on. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for this part.

The scheme's value point: the direction of the induced current in the ring is such that the polarity developed in the ring is the SAME as that of the polarity on the face of the coil, hence it will jump up due to the repulsive force.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Closing the switch starts a current in the coil, which grows from zero to its steady value. The iron core concentrates the field, so the magnetic flux threading the copper ring rises rapidly. By Faraday's law that changing flux induces an emf round the ring, and since the ring is a closed conductor of low resistance a large induced current flows in it.

Lenz's law fixes the direction of that current: it must oppose the INCREASE in flux that is causing it. The ring therefore develops on its lower face the same magnetic polarity as the upper face of the solenoid beneath it. Like poles repel, so the ring is pushed upwards, and because the flux changes very quickly the force is large enough to throw it clear of the core.

The same conclusion can be reached without poles: the induced current circulates in the sense OPPOSITE to the current in the nearby turns of the coil, and antiparallel currents repel.

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem: What will happen if the terminals of the battery are reversed and the switch is closed ? Explain.
rows.context:
Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off.

Answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - same drawing as Q34 (a) (i); this sub-part names the battery terminals, which exist only in the figure. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for this part.

The scheme's value point: the polarity of the induced current in the ring will get REVERSED on changing the terminals of the battery, so the ring will jump again.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Reversing the battery reverses the current in the coil and hence the direction of its magnetic field. But the ring's response reverses with it: the flux through the ring now grows in the opposite direction, so by Lenz's law the induced current in the ring also reverses, and the ring's face nearest the solenoid again ends up with the SAME polarity as the solenoid face it is looking at.

The force is therefore repulsive once more and the ring jumps exactly as before, with the same magnitude. This is the point of the sub-part: Lenz's law depends on the change in flux OPPOSING itself, not on any absolute direction, so nothing an experimenter does to the battery polarity can turn the repulsion into an attraction while the current is being switched ON.

rows.stem: Explain the two laws that help us understand this phenomenon.
rows.context:
Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off.

Answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - same drawing as Q34 (a) (i); 'this phenomenon' is the set-up the figure defines. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 + 1 marks for the two laws.

Lenz's law (the scheme's value point): it states that the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux that produces it.

Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction (the scheme's value point): whenever there is a change in magnetic flux through a coil, an emf is induced. The magnitude of the induced emf in a coil is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Written together the two laws are the single equation

\(\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt}\),

in which Faraday's law supplies the magnitude and Lenz's law supplies the minus sign.

Each law does a distinct job in this experiment. Faraday's law explains why there is a current in the ring AT ALL: the ring is not connected to anything, and the only thing happening to it is that the flux through it is changing. Lenz's law explains why the ring is thrown UP rather than pulled down: the induced current must oppose the growth of flux, which forces the repulsive polarity.

Lenz's law is also a statement of the conservation of energy. If the ring were attracted, it would accelerate towards the coil and gain kinetic energy while the flux change that drives it also increased, giving energy out of nothing. Because it is repelled, the kinetic energy the ring flies off with has to be supplied by the battery, which does extra work against the induced back emf in the circuit.

rows.subtopic: Ampere's Circuital Law and the Solenoid
rows.stem: Briefly explain various ways to increase the strength of magnetic field produced by a given solenoid.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: this alternative carries 4 marks on the question paper, but the scheme allots it only "1 + 1" and prints just two ways (inserting a soft iron core, and increasing the current). Two one-mark value points cannot fill a four-mark answer, and the question asks for "various ways", not two. The scheme's two ways are given first and the remaining ways are added after, so that the answer is worth the marks the paper awards it.]

The scheme's value points: the strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid can be increased by INSERTING A SOFT IRON CORE inside the solenoid, and by INCREASING THE CURRENT in the solenoid.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Everything follows from the field inside a long solenoid,

\(B = \mu_0 n I = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{l}\),

where \(n = N/l\) is the number of turns per unit length. There are three independent quantities on the right, and each gives a way of raising \(B\).

1. INCREASE THE CURRENT. \(B\) is directly proportional to \(I\), so doubling the current doubles the field. This is the easiest lever in practice, and its limit is the heating of the winding, so thicker wire of lower resistance allows a larger current to be passed safely.

2. INCREASE THE NUMBER OF TURNS PER UNIT LENGTH. \(B\) is proportional to \(n\), not to \(N\) alone, so either wind more turns into the same length, by packing them closer or by winding several layers one over another, or keep the same number of turns and make the solenoid shorter.

3. INSERT A SOFT FERROMAGNETIC CORE. With a core of relative permeability \(\mu_r\) the field becomes

\(B = \mu_0\mu_r n I\),

and since \(\mu_r\) for soft iron runs from several hundred to several thousand, this multiplies the field by that factor and is by far the largest single increase available. SOFT iron is specified rather than steel because it loses its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off, which is what an electromagnet is wanted for.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem: Which light beam has the highest frequency and why ?
rows.context: Figure shows the variation of photoelectric current measured in a photo cell circuit as a function of the potential difference between the plates of the photo cell when light beams A, B, C and D of different wavelengths are incident on the photo cell. Examine the given figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the whole question is a reading of the graph. Vertical axis 'Current', horizontal axis 'Potential Difference' with a marked 0 and - to its left, + to its right; four labelled curves A, B, C and D each rising from the negative-potential region to their own saturation plateau, the labels stacked at the right-hand edge in the order A, B, C, D from top to bottom. Which curve cuts the axis furthest into the negative region - the stopping-potential comparison the three sub-parts all turn on - is deliberately NOT described. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 mark for the identification and 1/2 for the reason.

The scheme's value point: the light beam B, because it requires the maximum retarding potential to reduce the photoelectric current to zero.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Read the graph at the point where each curve meets the horizontal axis on the NEGATIVE side. That intercept is the stopping potential \(V_0\) for that beam, the retarding potential just sufficient to turn back even the fastest photoelectron. Of the four curves, the one labelled B cuts the axis furthest to the left, so its stopping potential is the largest in magnitude.

By Einstein's photoelectric equation, \(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\), and the metal is the same for all four beams, so \(\phi_0\) is fixed and \(V_0\) increases with the frequency alone. The largest stopping potential therefore belongs to the beam of highest frequency, which is the beam labelled B.

Note that the SATURATION currents, the heights of the four plateaus, are not the quantity to read here. They measure the intensity, that is the number of photons arriving per second, and say nothing about the energy of each photon.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem: Which light beam has the longest wavelength and why ?
rows.context: Figure shows the variation of photoelectric current measured in a photo cell circuit as a function of the potential difference between the plates of the photo cell when light beams A, B, C and D of different wavelengths are incident on the photo cell. Examine the given figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - same graph as Q35 (a) (i); the answer is read off the stopping potentials. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1/2 mark for the identification and 1/2 for the reason.

The scheme's value point: the light beam C, because it requires the minimum retarding potential to reduce the photoelectric current to zero.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

Wavelength and frequency are inversely related, \(\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu}\), so the beam of LONGEST wavelength is the beam of LOWEST frequency, and by \(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\) that is the beam with the SMALLEST stopping potential.

On the graph this is the curve whose negative intercept lies closest to the origin, which is the curve labelled C. Following the four curves through the two places where they cross one another, the four intercepts run, from the furthest left to the nearest the origin, in the order B, A, D, C. So the beam of highest frequency is the one labelled B, as in the previous part, while the beam of lowest frequency, and therefore of longest wavelength, is the one whose curve stops the photocurrent soonest.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Which light beam ejects photoelectrons with maximum momentum and why ?
rows.context: Figure shows the variation of photoelectric current measured in a photo cell circuit as a function of the potential difference between the plates of the photo cell when light beams A, B, C and D of different wavelengths are incident on the photo cell. Examine the given figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - same graph as Q35 (a) (i); the beam has to be identified from the curves. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 mark for the identification and 1 for the reason.

The scheme's value points: the light beam B ejects photoelectrons with maximum momentum, because the highest frequency light beam ejects photoelectrons with the highest kinetic energy and hence the highest momentum.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The chain of reasoning is:

\(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0 = eV_0\), and \(p_{max} = \sqrt{2mK_{max}} = \sqrt{2m\,eV_0}\).

Both steps are monotonic, so whichever beam has the largest stopping potential also has the largest maximum kinetic energy and therefore the largest maximum momentum. From the graph that is the beam labelled B, the same beam identified in the first sub-part.

The momentum grows only as the SQUARE ROOT of the stopping potential, so a beam with four times the stopping potential of another gives photoelectrons of only twice the momentum.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: What is the effect on threshold frequency and stopping potential on increasing the frequency of incident beam of light ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme allots 1 + 1 marks for the two effects with their justification.

The scheme's value points:

There is NO EFFECT on the threshold frequency, since it is a characteristic of the metal.

With an increase in the frequency of the incident beam of light, the STOPPING POTENTIAL INCREASES, because to stop photoelectrons of higher kinetic energy a larger retarding potential is required.

The scheme adds that full credit is to be given if a candidate explains the effect of frequency on stopping potential using the formula

\(eV_0 = h(\nu - \nu_0)\)

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

The threshold frequency is defined by \(h\nu_0 = \phi_0\), where \(\phi_0\) is the work function, that is, the minimum energy needed to pull an electron out of that particular metal. The work function is a property of the METAL and of its surface, so nothing done to the incident light can change it. Shining a higher-frequency beam on the same plate leaves \(\nu_0\) exactly where it was.

The stopping potential, by contrast, measures the energy of the photoelectrons, not of the metal. Rearranging Einstein's equation,

\(V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\),

so a graph of \(V_0\) against \(\nu\) is a straight line of slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\), the same for every metal, cutting the frequency axis at \(\nu_0\) and the potential axis at \(-\dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\). Raising \(\nu\) therefore raises \(V_0\) LINEARLY, and each extra photon energy \(h\Delta\nu\) is handed straight to the ejected electron, because the amount spent on escaping the surface is fixed.

It is worth separating this from the effect of INTENSITY, which the question does not ask about but which is the common confusion: raising the intensity at fixed frequency raises the saturation current, since more photons arrive each second, and leaves the stopping potential untouched.
